result with a fix found by it.

## What this module is, and what it is not

A TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) server for the collection, built as a buffer-driven (sans-I/O) core with
a blocking wrapper on top, on the `tls13` handshake building blocks (key schedule,
CertificateVerify, key exchange, transcript) and the collection's AEADs (`aesgcm`,
`chachapoly`). It is built to replace the web-server consumer's fork of a third-party TLS server.

**What it does:** `Server`, a sans-I/O full handshake — ClientHello → ServerHello, compatibility CCS,
EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished → the client's Finished — then
application data both ways and close_notify, over the record layer (header, in-place protection,
the receive side, alerts), the ClientHello decoder and the message encoders. It handshakes with
OpenSSL 3.5's `s_client` (ECDSA P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, RSA-PSS and ML-DSA-65
certificates; all three suites; X25519MLKEM768, X25519, secp256r1, secp384r1, ML-KEM-1024;
ALPN; with and without SNI), with Go's
crypto/tls client (the same, Go's own defaults), with `tlsclient` and with Zig std's client;
`Connection` drives it over a `std.Io.Reader`/`Writer` pair; `keys.CertKeyPair` loads the
certificate chain and private key from PEM. A client that sent no share for the chosen group
gets a HelloRetryRequest. After the handshake KeyUpdate works both ways: a client's turns the
receive key over (and `update_requested` is answered once), the server rekeys on its own at
`max_records_per_key` (2^23 records, asking the client to rekey too) or when the application
calls `keyUpdate`; at most `max_key_updates` (32) KeyUpdates may come between two
application-data records (rustls, BoringSSL); only a record with data refills that budget, an empty
application-data record does not (BoringSSL `kMaxKeyUpdates`, `src/server.zig`). With `Config.tickets` it issues NewSessionTickets
and resumes them (below). With `Config.client_auth` it asks for a client certificate, verifies
the chain (`ClientCertVerifier`; `X509Verifier` = `x509.verifyChain` with clientAuth) and the
client's CertificateVerify, and reports the leaf (`peerCertificate`), resumptions included. The seams the web-server consumer's zero-copy codecs need are in:
one send buffer, `Connection.reader()` / `writer()` in place, `Server.writeSlot` / `commitWrite`. `reader()`'s buffer is
one record, so std's delimiter helpers search one record: with nothing buffered the first call loads a record and returns
`StreamTooLong` (std's exit for a full buffer); `peekGreedy(1)` first makes them answer (doc comment, tested).

**Never in scope:** TLS 1.2 and earlier, and DTLS (the `dtls` module). **Not in v1:** kTLS itself (the
record keys can be handed over to it: `Server.extractSecrets`) and post-handshake client authentication (*What is deliberately not
done*).

## Wire format / algorithm

### Certificate and key loading (`keys.zig`)

`CertKeyPair.fromPem(out, gpa, chain_pem, key_pem)`: every `CERTIFICATE` block of `chain_pem`
(leaf first; blocks of other labels skipped, so one combined file can serve as both arguments,
and a file concatenated without a final newline still splits), and the first private-key block
of `key_pem`:

| Label | Content | Keys |
|---|---|---|
| `EC PRIVATE KEY` | RFC 5915 ECPrivateKey; the `[0]` curve required | P-256, P-384, P-521 |
| `PRIVATE KEY` | RFC 5958 PrivateKeyInfo / OneAsymmetricKey (v0 or v1) | EC P-256/P-384/P-521 (a `[0]` inside must agree; absent AlgorithmIdentifier parameters take the `[0]` curve, as Go does), Ed25519 (RFC 8410: no parameters, a 32-octet seed), RSA (keycodec reads the PKCS#8 shell, `rsa.SecretKey.fromDer` the PKCS#1 inside), ML-DSA-44/65/87 (RFC 9881: no parameters; the `seed` and `both` forms — `both` must match its seed; `expandedKey` alone is `UnsupportedKey`, as only its public half could be checked against the leaf) |
| `RSA PRIVATE KEY` | PKCS#1 RSAPrivateKey | RSA (`rsa.SecretKey.fromDer`: two-prime, consistency-checked) |
| `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY`, or any key with RFC 1421 `Proc-Type` headers; `OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY` | — | refused, `UnsupportedKey` |
| any of the above, malformed | — | `MalformedKey`: strict DER throughout (a field or byte after the key's last element, an attribute not shaped `SEQUENCE { OID, SET }`, an ML-DSA key part of the wrong length); explicit EC parameters (a `[0]` or AlgorithmIdentifier holding no curve OID) are `UnsupportedKey` |

The PEM walk, the base64 decode and the DER structure (strict DER, version, algorithm identifier,
every length, the EC scalar range) are the `keycodec` module's (`parsePrivateKeyPem`); this file maps its parts onto the signing key types and checks what keycodec leaves
to the key type (an ML-DSA `both` key's halves, the key against the leaf).

An EC scalar shorter than the order is left-padded (as OpenSSL reads it); longer, zero or ≥ the
order is `MalformedKey` (std's `SecretKey.fromBytes` checks nothing, so the range is checked
here). Every chain entry must be readable by `x509.spkiOf`, not merely DER
(`MalformedCertificate`); an END line must name its BEGIN's label (`InvalidPem`); CRLF is
accepted. An RSA key under an id-RSASSA-PSS leaf is `UnsupportedKey`. Other curves (P-521, secp256k1) and algorithms are `UnsupportedKey`.
The key must belong to the leaf (`x509.spkiOf`: algorithm, named curve, and the public key
derived from the private one equal to the certificate's), else `KeyMismatch` — rustls's
`keys_match`, Go's `X509KeyPair`. DER is read strictly: definite lengths, minimal length
octets, at most two length octets. `certifiedKey()` borrows from the pair (it must not move);
`deinit` wipes the key and frees.

**The handshake** (`server.Server`, RFC 8446 §2 Figure 1, full handshake): the caller feeds
received octets (`feed` → `need_more`, `handshake_done`, `app_data`, `peer_closed`, and how much
was consumed) and drains `pendingOutput`. On the ClientHello, in rustls 0.23's order and with its
alerts: compression must include null (`illegal_parameter`); an invalid SNI is
`illegal_parameter`; no `signature_algorithms` is `handshake_failure`; no TLS 1.3 in
`supported_versions` is `protocol_version`; the certificate is fixed or chosen by
`CertificateSelector` from the SNI (`access_denied` when none); the signature scheme is the key's
first candidate the client offers (or, with `CertifiedKey.signature_schemes`, the first of
those the key can make and the client offers); the suite is the client's first enabled one; the
group is the client's first `supported_groups` entry the server enables (with
`Config.server_order`, suite and group go by the server's lists instead, BoringSSL
`SSL_OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE`; `Config.server_suite_order` does that for the suite only,
so the group still follows the client and costs no HelloRetryRequest) — every one of these without a match
is `handshake_failure`; compression other than exactly null is `illegal_parameter`; no
`key_share` is `handshake_failure`, two shares of one group or a share that does not exchange
(`kex`: wrong length, low order) `illegal_parameter`, no share for the chosen group
gets a HelloRetryRequest (below); `pre_shared_key` without `psk_key_exchange_modes` is
`missing_extension` (otherwise, without `Config.tickets`, the offer is ignored: full handshake;
with it, see *Resumption*); ALPN is the server's first
protocol the client offers (`no_application_protocol` when the server has some and none match).
The server then sends ServerHello (plaintext), a compatibility CCS, and under its handshake key
EncryptedExtensions (the ALPN choice; an empty `server_name` acknowledging a DNS-name SNI),
Certificate (on the leaf, an OCSP staple if the client sent `status_request` of type ocsp and
an SCT list if it sent `signed_certificate_timestamp`, each when configured and non-empty),
CertificateVerify and
Finished, one record per message; it switches its sending key to the application secret and
waits for the client's Finished (`decrypt_error` if it does not verify), after which application
data flows. Early data is taken only with `Config.early_data` (*0-RTT* below); otherwise records
the client sent under a 0-RTT key are skipped (up to 2^14 octets, or `EarlyData.max_size`). Every refusal queues its alert in `pendingOutput` (sealed once the server
sends protected) and leaves the connection dead (`error.Closed` afterwards); every key and secret
is wiped at that moment. `close` queues close_notify and keeps reading.

**Resumption** (RFC 8446 §2.2, §4.2.11, §4.6.1; rustls 0.23 rules, `Config.tickets`). After
the client's Finished the server sends `Tickets.count` (2) NewSessionTickets packed into one
record — none when the client did not offer `psk_dhe_ke`, the only mode served (no `psk_ke`).
A client's RFC 9149 `ticket_request` sets the count instead: its `new_session_count` after a full
handshake, its `resumption_count` after a resumption, at most `Tickets.max_requested` (2), and the
EncryptedExtensions echo the count in their own `ticket_request` (rustls `Tls13Tickets`, which
resolves and echoes it the same way); a request that is not two octets is `decode_error`.
Each ticket is a `Ticketer` blob (`StekTicketer`: `tlsresume`'s AES-256-GCM STEK ring, key id
as AAD, keys past the rotation policy's lifetime refused) over `tlsresume.select.SessionState`
(resumption master secret over the transcript through the client's Finished, a one-octet nonce
= the ticket's index, issue time, `ticket_age_add`) followed by this server's `TicketFields`:
format 2, SNI, ALPN, the client's certificate (DER leaf, ≤ `ClientAuth.max_leaf_len`; empty
without one) and
the scheme it signed with, suite — the suite last, read from the end, so a SHA-384 ticket opened
with a SHA-256 prefix can never match the negotiated suite. `ticket_lifetime` is
`min(Tickets.lifetime_s, 7 days)` (12 h by default, rustls), and each ticket carries an empty
GREASE extension (RFC 8701 §3.2, as BoringSSL). A ticket that cannot be sealed or has no room
in the output is not sent, nor are the rest. On a ClientHello with `pre_shared_key` (the second
one after a HelloRetryRequest; the first is not looked at), `tlsresume.select.selectPsk`
takes the first of up to 32 identities that opens, is younger than 7 days and the configured
lifetime, has the negotiated suite and the same SNI (rustls `can_resume`; the client's reported
age is not checked — it matters only for early data); that identity's binder over
`Truncate(ClientHello)` (after `message_hash` and the HelloRetryRequest when there was one) must
verify — otherwise `decrypt_error` (RFC 8446 §4.2.11 MUST; a binder of the wrong length counts
as wrong) — and nothing is decided before it, the binder of a ticket not taken is never looked
at; as in rustls the binder is checked before the PSK modes are, so a bad binder with only
`psk_ke` offered is still `decrypt_error`. The resumed handshake: ServerHello with `pre_shared_key` (the index) and a key share (a
fresh (EC)DHE always runs), early secret from the PSK, EncryptedExtensions without the SNI
acknowledgement (RFC 6066 §3), no Certificate or CertificateVerify, Finished; `isResumed()`.
A ticket's plaintext is built around the leaf where it lies in the caller's peer buffer
(below), and opened there — a ticket whose leaf is over this connection's cap is not resumed,
nor one with a leaf when there is no client authentication — and the sealed blob goes straight
into its place in the output: no copy of the leaf, no ticket-sized stack array. Every buffer
holding the resumption secret, the PSK or a ticket's plaintext is wiped before the step returns.
**Stateful tickets** (RFC 8446 §2.2's database lookup; rustls's default `session_storage`):
`CacheTicketer` keeps the plaintext in a `tlsresume.SessionCache` (`SessionCache(max_leaf_len)`:
fixed entries of `ticketStateLen(max_leaf_len)` octets, oldest-first eviction, timeout, no lock)
under a random 32-octet id that is the ticket; opening takes the entry out (rustls `take`), so a
ticket resumes at most once, binder good or not, and its `replayGuard()` admits every early-data
ticket (a replayed ClientHello finds no session). Costs of single use (rustls has them too): the
id crosses the wire in the clear, so whoever saw a ClientHello can spend its ticket with a bad
binder; a flood of full handshakes evicts real sessions; every lookup scans the whole cache (up to
32 identities per ClientHello). Entries are sized by the configuration's `max_leaf_len` (a
smaller cache issues no ticket to a longer leaf). Not done: the ticket count request (RFC 9149, *Backlog*).

**0-RTT early data** (RFC 8446 §2.3, §4.2.10, §4.5, §8; opt-in `Config.early_data`, with
tickets). Each NewSessionTicket carries `early_data` with `EarlyData.max_size` (BoringSSL's
14336 by default) before its GREASE extension, and the ticket records that size (ticket format
3; older tickets resume nothing). A resumed ClientHello's early data is taken, in BoringSSL's
order of reasons (`EarlyDataReason`, `Server.earlyDataReason`): `disabled` (no `early_data`
configuration, `max_size` 0 or no tickets), `no_session_offered`, `session_not_resumed`,
`hello_retry_request` (the first ClientHello offered it and was retried), `peer_declined`,
`unsupported_for_session` (a ticket issued without it), `not_first_identity`, `alpn_mismatch`
(the protocol negotiated is not the ticket's), `ticket_age_skew` (`|ticketAgeSkew()|` over
`max_age_skew_s`, 60 s as BoringSSL and rustls), then `replayed` — the `ReplayGuard` is asked
last and only once (single-use tickets, RFC 8446 §8.1; `strikeRegisterGuard` over a
`tlsresume.replay.StrikeRegister`, whose window must be at least twice `max_age_skew_s`, since
a recording stays within the skew for up to that long). Taken: the EncryptedExtensions carry an
empty `early_data`, the receive key is the client's early traffic secret (over the complete
ClientHello), `feed` returns `early_data_accepted` and then `early_data` events (0-RTT data,
replayable) up to the ticket's `max_early_data_size` and the configured one, whichever is less
(more is `unexpected_message`); the server may write half-RTT data (`canWrite`). The client's
EndOfEarlyData must be empty (`decode_error`), a message of its own ending its record
(`unexpected_message`), and switches the receive key to the client's handshake secret; any
other handshake message in the early state is `unexpected_message`. A close_notify sent
half-RTT ends the writing: no ticket follows the client's Finished. Unlike rustls (stateful
tickets only, `send_half_rtt_data` off by default) early data rides on stateless tickets with a
replay guard, and half-RTT writes are always allowed once early data is taken (as BoringSSL).
`Connection.handshake` returns once early data is taken (`server.inEarlyData()`); `read`
returns it and completes the handshake.

**Exporter** (RFC 8446 §7.5, RFC 5705's interface): `Server.exportKeyingMaterial(out, label,
context)` fills `out` with `HKDF-Expand-Label(Derive-Secret(exporter_master_secret, label, ""),
"exporter", Hash(context), out.len)`. The `exporter_master_secret` is derived with the
application secrets (over the transcript through the server's Finished) and kept for the
connection's life — wiped by `deinit` or a failure, unlike the master secret, which goes with
the client's Finished. It answers once `canWrite()` holds: the handshake completed, or early
data was taken and the server writes half-RTT data (BoringSSL `SSL_export_keying_material`;
BoGo `ExportKeyingMaterial-Server-HalfRTT`) — the client's Finished, and its certificate, are
then still to come; before that `HandshakeNotComplete`. No context and an empty one are the
same value (§7.5), so there is one form. Refused: a label over `max_exporter_label_len` (249,
`HkdfLabel`'s 255 less `"tls13 "`: `LabelTooLong`), an output over `maxExporterLen(suite)` (255
HKDF blocks: 8160 octets with SHA-256, 12240 with SHA-384: `OutputTooLong`). RFC 5705's reserved
labels are TLS 1.2's PRF labels and not checked (rustls neither). The derivation is
`tls13.keyschedule`'s (`Schedule.exportKeyingMaterial`, run-time length, burned). Not done: the
early exporter (`early_exporter_master_secret`, RFC 8446 §7.5's 0-RTT variant; rustls has none
on the server).

**Record size limit** (RFC 8449; rustls and Go have none — rustls only a configured
`max_fragment_size`; NSS/Firefox send it). A client's `record_size_limit` (64 or more, else
`illegal_parameter`; not two octets, `decode_error`) bounds every protected record the server
sends from the EncryptedExtensions on: TLSInnerPlaintext (content and type octet) at most the
limit, clamped to 2^14 + 1, so content at most limit − 1 (`write`, tickets and alerts included;
`Config.max_fragment_len` still applies when lower). The ServerHello and the CCS go in the clear
as they are (§4: unprotected records are not limited). The EncryptedExtensions answer with the
server's own limit, 2^14 + 1 (what it receives). A second ClientHello must repeat the first's
(present or not, same value: `illegal_parameter`). Not in QUIC (no records). `minOutputLen`
sizes for 63-octet records. `peerRecordSizeLimit()` reports it. Checked by tlsfuzzer's
`test-record-size-limit.py` (every TLS 1.3 case, `tools/tlsfuzzer/baseline.tsv`).

**Dynamic record sizing** (Go `crypto/tls`, on by default there; s2n
`s2n_connection_set_dynamic_record_threshold`; rustls has none). With `Config.dynamic_records`,
application data records start at one TCP segment — `segment_len`, 1186 octets of content: Go's
1208-octet estimate less a TLS 1.3 record's 22 octets — and grow as Go's do: record k (from 0)
carries at most `segment_len × (k + 1)`, up to `max_fragment_len` (or the client's record size
limit), and every record is full once `boost_after` (128 KiB) went out. The client can decrypt
the first octets of a response from the first segment instead of waiting for 16 KiB. With a
`clock`, a writer idle for `idle_reset_ms` (1 s) starts small again (s2n; Go never does).
`Server.recordLen()` is the next record's length; `write` and `writeSlot` keep to it, and
`Connection`'s writer seals records of that length. Off by default (a server tuned for bulk
throughput would pay ~1.8 % more record overhead in the first 128 KiB).

**Encrypted Client Hello** (RFC 9849, `ech`, `Config.ech`; Go and BoringSSL and picotls
serve it, rustls does not: its BoGo config says "ECH server support NYI"). The client
encrypts its real ClientHello (the inner, with the real SNI, ALPN and tickets) to the
server's ECH key inside an outer one naming a public name. `ech.Ech.keys` are `ECHConfig`s
(version 0xfe0d) with their X25519 private keys; served: DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256) with
HKDF-SHA256 and AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 (`hpke`). `ech.makeConfig`
and `ech.configList` build a config and the `ECHConfigList` for a DNS HTTPS record;
`Ech.check` validates the keys. On the first ClientHello the key with the offer's
config_id and suite opens the payload — HPKE `SetupBaseR(enc, sk, "tls ech" ‖ 0 ‖ config)`,
`Open(outer hello with the payload zeroed, payload)` — and the inner hello is rebuilt in the
caller's ECH buffer (`Server.setEchBuffer`, `ech.bufferLen(max_client_hello_len)`): the
outer session id in, `ech_outer_extensions` replaced by the outer extensions it names, in
one forward pass (missing, repeated, out of order or `encrypted_client_hello` itself:
`EchInvalidOuterExtension`; non-zero padding or an inner session id: `EchInvalidPadding`;
all `illegal_parameter`). The inner hello must carry an inner offer and offer nothing
below TLS 1.3 (`EchInvalidInner`). From then on the handshake is the inner hello's
(transcript, certificate choice, PSKs, early data, ALPN, JA4 aside: JA4 is the outer's,
the one on the wire); the ServerHello's last 8 random octets carry
`HKDF-Expand-Label(HKDF-Extract(0, inner.random), "ech accept confirmation", transcript, 8)`.
A HelloRetryRequest carries the "hrr ech accept confirmation" in its own
`encrypted_client_hello`; the second outer hello must offer again with the same
config_id and suite and an empty `enc` (`EchOfferChanged`, `illegal_parameter`;
none at all: `missing_extension`), its payload opens under the same HPKE context
(sequence 1; failing: `EchDecryptionFailed`, `decrypt_error`). An offer that opens with
no key (a GREASE offer, a stale config, a hello over `max_client_hello_len`) is not an
error: the outer hello goes on (its SNI picks the public name's certificate) and the
EncryptedExtensions carry `retry_configs`, the keys marked `retry`. A hello with an
inner offer and no outer one gets the confirmation too (the backend's part in split
mode, as BoringSSL — only on a server without ECH keys: a client-facing one refuses an
inner offer with `illegal_parameter`, RFC 9849 §7). `Server.echAccepted()` reports it. Checked by: BoGo's 45 TLS
`ECH-Server-*` tests (accept, decline with retry configs, HRR, outer extensions and their
faults, padding, ciphers, early data, client certificates, backend role; the shim's
`-ech-server-config/-key/-is-retry-config`, `-expect-ech-accept`), Go 1.26's ECH client
live and replayed byte-exact (`go-ech`, `go-ech-hrr`, `go-ech-resume*`), and the
`tlsserver-ech` fuzz harness (the inner hello rebuilt from a model, every fault refused
with its error). Not done: split mode as a client-facing server (forwarding the inner
hello), ECH over DTLS, `ECHConfig` extensions (ignored, none is mandatory today),
HKDF-SHA384/512 and non-X25519 KEMs.

**Delegated credentials** (RFC 9345, `delegated`, `CertifiedKey.delegated_credential`;
BoringSSL serves them, rustls and Go do not; Firefox takes them). A credential is a
short-lived key the certificate's key signed: the edge holds only it, valid at most 7 days
past the leaf's notBefore. A `CertifiedKey` with `delegated_credential` has the issuing
chain, the credential's key (`key`, or `offload`) and the `DelegatedCredential`
(`delegated.issue` makes one; `keys.CertKeyPair.fromPemDelegated` loads its key, matched
against the credential's SubjectPublicKeyInfo). It is usable only with a client whose
`delegated_credential` extension offers its `dc_cert_verify_algorithm` and whose
`signature_algorithms` offer the leaf's signature over it (BoringSSL's rule; otherwise
`firstUsableKey` moves to the next key, and a lone credential is `handshake_failure`); it
then travels as the leaf's `delegated_credential` extension (in the RFC 8879 digest and
compressed forms too) and the CertificateVerify is the credential key's. `check` parses
it (at most 7 days, ECDSA or Ed25519 only, as BoringSSL; not with a raw public key);
`checkDelegated`, once at load, also verifies the leaf's signature (RFC 9345 §4: 64
spaces, the context string, 0, the leaf's DER, `cred`, `algorithm`) and that `key` is the
credential's (`checkDelegatedKey` without the signature). DelegationUsage on the leaf is
the client's check (BoringSSL's server makes none): `delegated.hasDelegationUsage`.
Checked by BoGo's `DelegatedCredentials-*` server tests (basic, both algorithm fields,
multiple credentials, key mismatch, RSA refused) — the shim takes BoringSSL's
credential list (`-new-x509-credential`, `-new-delegated-credential`,
`-expect-selected-credential`), which also runs 21 `CertificateSelection-Server-*` tests.
**Finding:** BoGo's runner signs and verifies credentials over leaf ‖ `algorithm` ‖
`cred` (`delegatedCredentialSignedMessage`), RFC 9345 §4 over leaf ‖ `cred` ‖
`algorithm`; BoringSSL's own server never computes it (it sends what it is given), so
only BoGo's credentials are affected. `delegated` follows the RFC; the shim checks the
key and the algorithm, not the signature.

**Connection migration** (`Server.serialize` / `deserialize`; s2n
`s2n_connection_serialize`, rustls none). A connected server's state — the application
traffic secrets and the exporter's, both sequence numbers, the KeyUpdate budget, suite,
group, ALPN, SNI, the client's certificate and how it was proved, resumption and early-data
outcome, ECH, the client's record size limit, JA4 — sealed into a blob under the caller's
32-octet key and to a `context` the caller names (AES-256-GCM, a random nonce, the AAD
"tlsserver connection v1" ‖ version ‖ context; `serializedLen` / `blobLen`), so a
restart, an upgrade or another process takes the connection over without the client
noticing (the web-server consumer: zero-downtime reload with the socket handed over). Unlike s2n's plaintext
blob, which its documentation tells the caller to encrypt and MAC, this one is sealed
already; a flipped octet, a wrong key, another context or another version is `BadBlob`.
**A blob is single-use:** two live copies seal different records under one key and
sequence number (AES-GCM nonce reuse), so the context should name the connection and the
hand-over's generation, and keeping a blob from being resumed twice or rolled back is
the caller's (the old server is finished; `deserialize` consumes the blob, wiping its
secrets). It needs `Config.enable_secret_extraction`, as `extractSecrets` does, and
`config.random` must be a CSPRNG (it draws the nonce). `Connection.serialize` refuses
while `reader()` holds decrypted octets or `writer()` unflushed ones. Conditions are
`extractSecrets`'s (output sent, every received octet fed — octets the caller holds
unconsumed travel with the blob, no KeyUpdate due), and the old server is finished
afterwards (one live copy: record nonces never repeat). `deserialize(out, config,
buffers, blob, key)` needs a configuration offering the same ALPN protocol
(`ConfigMismatch`) and a peer buffer for a blob with a client certificate; the rest of
the configuration is the new one's. Checked by: through `tlsclient` in every suite, a
connection with a client certificate and ALPN moved to a new `Server` on fresh buffers —
data both ways, the exporter's value unchanged, a KeyUpdate both ways, close — and every
refusal. Blobs are for builds of one tlsserver version.

**JA4 fingerprint** (`fingerprint.ja4`, FoxIO's `technical_details/JA4.md`; JA4 is
BSD-3-Clause, the other JA4+ methods are under the FoxIO License and are not implemented; s2n
offers JA3/JA4, rustls only a `ClientHello` view). The 36-character `a_b_c` fingerprint of a
parsed ClientHello: transport, version (highest `supported_versions`), SNI or not, suite and
extension counts, ALPN's first and last character; SHA-256 prefixes of the sorted suites and of
the sorted extensions (without SNI and ALPN) with the signature algorithms in order; GREASE left
out everywhere. Allocation-free; a hello with more than 512 suites or extensions has none.
`Config.ja4` keeps the first ClientHello's for `Server.ja4()`; a `CertificateSelector` can call
`fingerprint.ja4` on the `ClientHello` it gets and refuse the client before anything is sent.
`hello.ClientHello.extensions_raw` is the checked extension block. Anchored on the
specification's worked example (`t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1`, its two hashes
recomputed independently), with GREASE and shuffled order added. A differential check against
Wireshark's JA4 field is open (*Backlog*).

**Offloaded signing** (BoringSSL `SSL_PRIVATE_KEY_METHOD`, s2n `s2n_async_pkey`, picotls
`ptls_async_job_t`; rustls signs synchronously inside the handshake, `Signer::sign`). A
`CertifiedKey` with `key = null` and `offload = .{ .schemes = … }` holds no private key: the
scheme is the first of `Offload.schemes` the client offers (of those `certverify` knows), and a
full handshake stops after queueing ServerHello, CCS, EncryptedExtensions, CertificateRequest and
Certificate — `feed` returns `signature_needed` (and again, consuming nothing, until the
signature comes), `signatureRequest()` gives the scheme and RFC 8446 §4.4.3's content (64
spaces, the server's context string, a zero octet, the transcript hash), `provideSignature(sig)`
queues the CertificateVerify and the Finished and the handshake goes on in the state it would
have; `signatureFailed()` fails it with `internal_error`. With `Offload.verify` (the default; s2n's
`S2N_ASYNC_PKEY_VALIDATION_STRICT`) the signature is verified under the leaf's public key first, a
wrong one is `internal_error` here instead of `decrypt_error` at the client; an empty or over-long
one is always refused. The server's handshake traffic secret waits in the server for the
Finished (wiped with the other handshake secrets, and once used). A resumption signs nothing.
The flight up to the Certificate can go out while the key signs (the blocking `Connection` sends
it first, then calls its `signer`; without one the handshake fails with `SignatureNeeded`). QUIC
the same way (`quicFeed` reports `signature_needed`). `tls13.certverify.signContent` is the
signing for a signer that holds the key (re-exported as `tlsserver.certverify`). Checked by:
every key kind × suite through `tlsclient`, after a HelloRetryRequest and with a client
certificate; and BoGo's 49 `*-Async` tests, which the shim runs with the key offloaded and
`Connection.signer`.

**Client certificates** (RFC 8446 §4.3.2, §4.4.2, §4.4.3; rustls 0.23 rules,
`Config.client_auth`). A full handshake sends a CertificateRequest after the
EncryptedExtensions: an empty context, `ClientAuth.schemes` as `signature_algorithms` (rustls's
list by default: ECDSA P-384/P-256, Ed25519, RSA-PSS, then RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 for the chain only),
the CA names of `ClientAuth.authorities` as `certificate_authorities` when there are any; a
resumption sends none. The client's Certificate (`clientauth.parseCertificate`, checked whole):
malformed is `decode_error`; another context `illegal_parameter`; an entry with any extension
`unsupported_extension` (the request asks for none). Empty: `certificate_required` when
`ClientAuth.mandatory` (the default), otherwise the client goes on unauthenticated (no
CertificateVerify). Otherwise: at most 16 certificates and a leaf of at most
`ClientAuth.max_leaf_len` octets (4096 by default; `bad_certificate` past either); the leaf's
key must be one `certverify` verifies (RSA, ECDSA P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519, ML-DSA — the last
two only with their schemes in `ClientAuth.schemes`; an ML-DSA-65/87 leaf, 5.5-7.5 KB, needs a
larger `max_leaf_len`; an Ed25519 or ML-DSA key whose AlgorithmIdentifier carries parameters is
`bad_certificate`, RFC 8410 §3 / RFC 9881 §2, as for the server's own key and in Go) and its `keyUsage`,
if present, must assert `digitalSignature`
(`unsupported_certificate`; BoringSSL checks this in the TLS layer whatever the verifier says,
read from an `x509.safe`-vetted copy, made where the leaf is kept); then the chain, leaf first, goes to
`ClientCertVerifier.verify` with the `ClientAuth.clock` time, whose refusal names the alert
(`bad_certificate`, `unsupported_certificate`, `certificate_revoked`, `certificate_expired`,
`unknown_ca`, `access_denied`, `certificate_unknown`). `X509Verifier` is RFC 5280 path
validation to the caller's anchors with the clientAuth extended key usage
(`x509.verifyChain`, rustls `WebPkiClientVerifier`); the leaf's names are the application's
business. The CertificateVerify over the transcript through the client's Certificate: a scheme
the server did not ask for, RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (RFC 8446 §4.4.3) or one that does not suit the
leaf's key is `illegal_parameter`, a signature that does not verify `decrypt_error`. Then the
client's Finished as before. `peerCertificate()` is the leaf once its CertificateVerify verified
(never before), `peerSignatureScheme()` its scheme. `peerCertificates()` is the whole chain the
client sent, leaf first (rustls `peer_certificates`, Go `PeerCertificates`), when the caller gave a
buffer for the certificates after the leaf (`setPeerChainBuffer`; one that cannot take them is
`bad_certificate`, the joiner's message cap always can); without one, the leaf. Tickets carry the
leaf and the scheme, so a resumption reports the identity of the handshake that issued its ticket
(rustls keeps the whole chain in its tickets; here only the leaf, and so after `deserialize`). With a mandatory certificate a ticket without one is not resumed (a full handshake
asks for the certificate; rustls resumes it). A ticket also carries when the certificate was
proved, carried across re-issued tickets: past the ticket lifetime from that full handshake the
ticket is not resumed, however young it is — so an expired or revoked certificate does not live
on through resumptions (rustls re-issues indefinitely). A failed handshake reports no identity.

**Raw public keys** (RFC 7250). `CertifiedKey.raw_public_key` makes the server's certificate its key's DER
SubjectPublicKeyInfo (`chain[0]`, rustls `only_raw_public_keys`), sent only to a client that offers RawPublicKey in
`server_certificate_type`. `ClientAuth.raw_public_keys` (a `clientauth.RawKeyVerifier`) authenticates a client by a raw
key instead of a chain, only when it offers RawPublicKey in `client_certificate_type`; `peerCertificate` is then the
key's DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo and `peerRawPublicKey()` is true. A resumption does not ask the raw-key verifier again,
and a resuming client must offer RawPublicKey again (as in rustls).

**Certificate compression** (RFC 8879; `CertifiedKey.compressed_certificates`; rustls and BoringSSL compress per
handshake, here no compressor runs in the handshake and the module gains no dependency). The caller compresses the
Certificate message ahead of time: `CertifiedKey.uncompressedCertificate(out, staples)` → any compressor → one
`CompressedCertificate` per algorithm and per set of staples, in the caller's order of preference. The handshake sends
the first whose algorithm the client offers and whose staples are the ones this handshake sends, else the Certificate
uncompressed. `check` refuses an entry whose `uncompressed_len` no longer matches (`CompressedStale`), and with the
entry's `digest` set (SHA-256 of the uncompressed message) any other change too; without it a same-length replacement
(a refreshed OCSP staple usually is one) is not seen, so the caller compresses again whenever it replaces the chain or
a staple (`src/server.zig`). Interop: OpenSSL 3.5 `s_client` decompresses a std-zlib entry; the BoGo
shim installs BoringSSL's three mock algorithms.

**QUIC mode** (RFC 9001; rustls `quic::ServerConnection`). `Config.quic`: CRYPTO data in and out per encryption level
(`quicFeed`, `quicOutput`), each level's traffic secret for the QUIC stack (`quicSecret`; packet keys via `quic-crypto`),
transport parameters both ways, 0-RTT with the stack's resumption data and a veto (`setQuicResumptionData`,
`Quic.accept_early`; the veto's reason is `quic_parameter_mismatch`), alerts as `quicAlert`. A QUIC ticket carries the
stack's resumption data and resumes over QUIC only (ticket formats `format_quic` / `format_quic_raw`,
`src/server.zig`); `pendingOutput` gives one level at a time. Offloaded signing works the same way (`quicFeed`
reports `signature_needed`).

**HelloRetryRequest** (RFC 8446 §4.1.4, rustls 0.23 rules): when the client sent no share for
the chosen group, the server fixes the suite, answers with a HelloRetryRequest naming the group
(no cookie) and a compatibility CCS, and restarts the transcript as
`message_hash(Hash(ClientHello1)) ‖ HelloRetryRequest` with the suite's hash (§4.4.1). The first
ClientHello must end its record flight (`unexpected_message`). The second must carry a share for
that group, the same SNI, still offer that suite, no `early_data`, and be the first hello but for
§4.1.2's changes (*Limits and refusals*) — otherwise `illegal_parameter`. Stricter than rustls, which re-chooses suite and group on the second hello
and compares only the hash: RFC 8446 §4.1.4/§4.2.8 bind both to the HelloRetryRequest; the ServerHello that follows has no second CCS.
Early data the first ClientHello announced is skipped in the clear up to 2^14 octets of
ciphertext, an empty record counting one octet (more: `unexpected_message`, as rustls). One compatibility CCS per ClientHello is
accepted (two in all).

**The blocking wrapper** (`connection.Connection`): the server over a `std.Io.Reader` /
`Writer`. Records are decrypted in place in the reader's own buffer (it must hold a whole
record), so `read` returns a slice of it, valid until the next read; pending output is flushed
before every wait, after the handshake, each `writeAll` and `close`; a refusal's alert is flushed
before the error is returned. A transport that ends before the handshake or mid-record is
`EndOfStream` (truncation). Reading sends too (what the server queued, before a read waits), so a reader and a writer
that may park while sending (fibers of one thread, an HTTP/2 stream per fiber) need a `Connection.Guard` (a mutex that
parks): it is held wherever the connection changes or sends its output and released while a read waits. Writers are still
serialised among themselves, there is one reader, `deinit` comes after every fiber is done with the connection, and `err`
holds whichever side's error came last. The guard does not make the connection safe across threads (`src/connection.zig`).

RFC 8446 §5, record layer over a byte stream:

- **Header** (`parseHeader`, `writeHeader`): `ContentType type ‖ uint16 legacy_record_version ‖
  uint16 length`, 5 octets. Protected records carry `application_data` (23) and `0x0303`.
- **Protection** (`Protection.seal` / `open`), per direction: `TLSInnerPlaintext = content ‖
  ContentType type ‖ zeros[pad]`, sealed with the suite's AEAD under the traffic key; nonce =
  the 12-byte IV XOR the 64-bit sequence number left-padded to 12 octets (§5.3); additional
  data = the record header (§5.2). The sequence number starts at 0 for every key and advances
  by one per record. Opening strips the zero padding and takes the last non-zero octet as the
  content type (§5.4).
- **Keys** (`Protection.init`): key and IV from the traffic secret by HKDF-Expand-Label "key" /
  "iv" (§7.3, `tls13.keyschedule.tls13.deriveTrafficKeyIv`), hash and key length per suite:

  | Suite | Code | Hash | Key | AEAD |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 | 0x1301 | SHA-256 | 16 | `aesgcm.Aes128Gcm.Context` |
  | TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 | 0x1302 | SHA-384 | 32 | `aesgcm.Aes256Gcm.Context` |
  | TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 | 0x1303 | SHA-256 | 32 | `chachapoly.ChaCha20Poly1305` |

  The AES suites keep an expanded `aesgcm` context per direction, so a record pays no key
  schedule (the fork's per-direction context, which the web-server consumer measured at 1.6–1.8× std at 16 KiB).
- **Receive side** (`inbound.Inbound.next`), sans-I/O: takes the received octets, returns one
  event — a whole handshake message, application data, `peer_closed` or `need_more` — and how
  many octets it is done with. Protected records are opened in place, so application data is a
  slice of the caller's buffer; handshake fragments are copied into a `Joiner` (caller's buffer,
  `Joiner.bufferLen(max_message)`, default cap 64 KiB as in rustls) which joins a message
  across records and splits several out of one. Rules (RFC 8446 §5; where it names no alert,
  rustls 0.23's choice):

  | Input | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Outer type not 20–23, version not `0x03XX`, empty non-`application_data` record | `decode_error` (header alone) |
  | Plaintext record > 2^14, protected > 2^14 + 256 | `record_overflow` (header alone) |
  | Handshake message over the joiner's cap | `decode_error` (its header alone) |
  | Another record type inside a fragmented handshake message | `unexpected_message` |
  | Receive key change with any handshake octet held (`installRx`) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext `change_cipher_spec` `0x01` after the first ClientHello, before the client Finished, ≤ 2 | dropped |
  | Any other CCS: before a ClientHello, after Finished, other content, a third one, protected | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext handshake or application data under a receive key; plaintext application data at all | `unexpected_message` |
  | Plaintext alert under a receive key after a protected record was opened, or > 2 octets | `unexpected_message` |
  | Zero-length protected handshake or alert content (§5.4) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Application data before the engine sets `app_data_ok` (no 0-RTT) | `unexpected_message` |
  | Alert content not two octets | `decode_error` |
  | Alert of unknown level | `illegal_parameter` |
  | Warning other than `close_notify`, `user_canceled` | `decode_error` |
  | `user_canceled` warning | ignored, 4 per connection, then `unexpected_message` |
  | `close_notify` after the handshake / before it | `peer_closed` (later octets ignored) / abort, no alert |
  | Fatal alert | abort, no alert (`peer_alert` holds it) |

  `inbound.alertFor` maps each error to the alert to send (none for the peer's own abort).
- **ClientHello** (`hello.parseClientHello`, RFC 8446 §4.1.2): zero-copy into slices of the
  message; lists stay in wire form and are walked by iterators that cannot fail (every length was
  checked). Extensions read: `server_name`, `status_request`, `supported_groups`,
  `ec_point_formats` (checked, unused), `signature_algorithms`, `signature_algorithms_cert`, ALPN,
  `compress_certificate`, `session_ticket` (skipped), `pre_shared_key`, `early_data`,
  `supported_versions`, `cookie`, `psk_key_exchange_modes`, `certificate_authorities` (checked),
  `key_share`, `renegotiation_info` (checked); others are skipped. Strictness is rustls 0.23's:

  | Input | Result |
  |---|---|
  | Any length that does not add up, trailing octets in an extension or the message | `decode_error` |
  | `legacy_session_id` > 32, empty or odd `cipher_suites`, no compression method | `decode_error` |
  | An empty list RFC 8446 / 6066 / 7301 declare non-empty (groups, signature schemes, versions, ALPN, ALPN name, cookie, PSK modes, PSK identities/binders, point formats) | `decode_error` |
  | `early_data` with a body; an empty SNI `host_name` | `decode_error` |
  | A repeated algorithm in `compress_certificate` (RFC 8879; BoringSSL, and rustls passes BoGo's `DuplicateCertCompressionExt`) | `decode_error` |
  | Any extension type twice (known, unknown or GREASE); `pre_shared_key` not last; PSK identities and binders of different counts | `illegal_parameter` |
  | An empty `key_share` list | accepted (the client asks for a HelloRetryRequest) |
  | No extension block at all | accepted (the state machine refuses it: no `supported_versions`) |

  SNI: a valid DNS name (rustls-pki-types rules: 1–253 octets, labels 1–63 of letters, digits,
  `_`, `-` not at a label's ends, an optional trailing dot, last label not all digits) is
  `dns_name`; an IP literal is `ip_address` and treated as no SNI; anything else, a second
  `host_name` or an empty list is `invalid` (the state machine answers `illegal_parameter`). A
  name type other than `host_name` ends the list. `pre_shared_key.binders_offset` is where the
  binder transcript ends (§4.2.11.2). Duplicate detection is an 8 KiB bit set over the whole
  type space, so it is linear in the number of extensions.
- **Server messages** (`messages`, RFC 8446 §4): ServerHello, HelloRetryRequest (the §4.1.3
  random), EncryptedExtensions, Certificate (entries with their extensions, e.g. an OCSP
  `status_request` on the leaf, §4.4.2.1), CertificateVerify and Finished, each returned whole
  (header ‖ body) from the caller's buffer; ALPN and OCSP extension bodies. ServerHello extension
  order is `pre_shared_key`, `key_share`, `cookie`, `supported_versions` (RFC 8448's). A field
  too long for its length prefix is `FieldTooLong`, a short buffer `BufferTooSmall`.
- **In place:** `seal` takes the content at `buf[5..]` and writes type, padding, tag and header
  around it; `open` decrypts over the ciphertext and returns a slice of the same buffer. That is
  the layout the web-server consumer's zero-copy record codecs read and write.

## Constant-time contract

**Key loading** (`keys`, through `keycodec`): the private key's PEM body is
decoded by `b64ct` (constant time) into a stack buffer that is wiped on every exit; the block
search walks block by block and skips a foreign body with a scan for its END line's first `-` (a
compare false on every base64 character), never a Boyer-Moore-Horspool `std.mem.find` over key
text (`keycodec.pem`). The DER walk branches on tags and lengths (the key's layout, not its
value); the
scalar range check is keycodec's borrow-chain compare (no branch on the scalar), the key-to-leaf
comparison std's and a `mem.eql` over public values.
`fromPem` runs under a 64 KiB burn (`burn.key_burn`; unburned 35 / 39 / 31 KiB for P-256 /
P-384 / Ed25519, an RSA parse burns its own below), held by `src/stackprobe_test.zig`. No
ctgrind row covers key loading.

Secrets: the traffic secret, the AEAD key state and the IV. The AEADs are the collection's
(`aesgcm` with its own ctgrind rows, `chachapoly`); the code here branches only on public
values — the suite, lengths, the sequence number, the tag verdict. The content-type scan in
`open` runs over the decrypted inner plaintext from its end and stops at the first non-zero
octet, so its time reveals the padding length; that is what rustls and OpenSSL do as well, and
the padding length is not a secret the record layer protects (padding hides the content length
from the wire, not from the receiver's timing). The `hs`, `app`, `ticket` and `ech` ctgrind rows (`src/ctgrind_harness.zig`) run the handshake,
the record layer, ticket handling and the decrypted ECH inner hello under tainted secrets.

Dead stack (`CONVENTIONS.md` §2.1.1): secrets in by `*const`, key state held in the caller's
`Protection`, wiped by `Protection.wipe`. `init` / `initKeyIv` run under a 1 KiB burn (their
HKDF and AES key expansion burn their own 8 KiB below); `seal` / `open` under 4 KiB
(`burn.record_burn`; AES-GCM in place reaches 1.2–1.4 KiB, ChaCha20-Poly1305 burns its own).
`Config.record_burn = false` (default true) skips the `seal` / `open` burn (~80 ns per record)
for a caller that scrubs the whole stack itself, e.g. at connection close; `Protection.burn_records`
carries it, set by `installTx` / `installRx`, and `init` resets it to true. `Protection.wipe`
zeroes with the vector `zeroize` (volatile stores, as `burn.stack`).
Measured and held by `src/stackprobe_test.zig` (ReleaseFast). `burn.handshake_burn` (16 KiB around each handshake step) is
held by a stack probe in `src/interop_replay_test.zig` that replays recorded handshakes (full, hybrid, HRR, resumed, mTLS,
RSA, P-384, Ed25519) through `Connection.handshake` in ReleaseFast; the client Certificate and CertificateVerify steps run
unburned (they touch no secret; their verifier frames reach deep), so the mTLS cases are probed for needles only
(`Expect.residue = false`, `src/interop_replay_test.zig`).

The receive side branches only on framing values (record types, lengths, the handshake header,
the alert octets). Decrypted application data stays in the caller's buffer; joined handshake
messages stay in the joiner's buffer until `Inbound.wipe`, which zeroes every octet the joiner
ever wrote and the receive key.
The send side likewise: `Outbound.wipe` (from `Server.deinit`) zeroes the send key and every
octet of the output buffer written since `init` — up to its high-water mark (`Outbound.dirty`:
content framed or refused by `commit`, `write`, and what `touch` reports), not the whole
buffer. A `writeSlot` not yet committed counts in full; `abandonWrite(n)` (what
`Connection.deinit` calls) narrows it to the `n` octets written. An encoder that fails
(`OutputFull`, `InternalError`) marks the whole buffer. Every per-connection wipe of a buffer
uses `zeroize` (volatile 32-byte stores): `std.crypto.secureZero` stores a byte at a time, and
wiping the web-server consumer's 48 KiB output that way cost ~16 µs a connection.

## Limits and refusals

The receive side's refusals are the table under *Wire format*. Record protection:

- `TLSInnerPlaintext` ≤ 2^14 + 1 octets (§5.2): `seal` refuses more (`RecordOverflow`), `open`
  refuses an authentic one that is larger (`RecordOverflow`, the `record_overflow` alert).
- `TLSCiphertext.length` ≤ 2^14 + 256 (§5.2): checked by `open` before any decryption
  (`RecordOverflow`). `max_record_len` (16,645) sizes a receive buffer for one whole record.
- A record shorter than a tag plus the type octet, or failing authentication: `BadRecordMac`
  (the `bad_record_mac` alert), with the ciphertext zeroed and the sequence number unchanged.
- A protected record whose outer type is not `application_data`: `UnexpectedRecordType`.
- An inner plaintext that is all zeros: `MissingContentType` (§5.4, `unexpected_message`).
- Sequence number 2^64 − 1: both directions refuse (`SequenceExhausted`); the engine must
  KeyUpdate first (§5.3). When to KeyUpdate earlier, at the AEAD's usage limit (§5.5), is the
  engine's policy: `Server` rekeys at `max_records_per_key` (2^23), the web-server consumer's bound.
- Records sent carry at most `Config.max_fragment_len` octets of content (2^14 by default,
  clamped to [512, 2^14]: rustls `max_fragment_size`, BoringSSL `SSL_set_max_send_fragment`);
  `minOutputLen` counts the extra records a smaller size makes. Records received may be 2^14.
- The send side keeps `alert_reserve` (24 octets) of the output buffer for one alert, so a fatal
  alert or close_notify can be queued however full the application left it.
- `Server.write` never cuts a record short to fit behind output still pending: it takes
  nothing (`OutputFull`) until the caller sends what waits, so record boundaries follow the
  data. An output below `full_record_output_len` (2^14 + 256 + 5 + 24) cuts records to what it
  holds even when empty.
- ClientHello: a `legacy_version` below 0x0301 is `protocol_version` even beside 0x0304 in
  `supported_versions` (RFC 8446 §D.5, OpenSSL; rustls ignores it). A key_share entry for a
  group missing from `supported_groups` (§4.2.8, a MAY) or for an obsolete_RESERVED group
  (§4.2.7) is `illegal_parameter`; obsolete groups in `supported_groups` alone are served
  (JDK 11 lists sect* and secp256k1 beside TLS 1.3, BoGo `Server-JDK11-*`), which
  tlsfuzzer's `test-tls13-obsolete-curves` (OpenSSL only with `--relaxed`) counts against.
- A client Finished of the wrong length is `decrypt_error`, as a wrong one (BoringSSL, rustls,
  BoGo `TrailingMessageData-TLS13-ClientFinished-TLS`); OpenSSL and tlsfuzzer want
  `decode_error`.
- A client certificate chain: at most `clientauth.max_chain_len` (16) certificates, a leaf of at
  most `ClientAuth.max_leaf_len` (default `clientauth.default_max_leaf_len`, 4096) octets
  (`bad_certificate`), the whole message within the joiner's cap (64 KiB by default,
  `decode_error`). The leaf is kept in a buffer the caller gives each `Server`
  (`setPeerBuffer`, `peerBufferLen(max_leaf_len)` octets: the leaf with room for a ticket's
  other fields around it and `x509.safe`'s padding after it), like the joiner's; under
  `client_auth` a missing or shorter one is `internal_error` at the ClientHello. Only the
  connections of a configuration with client authentication pay for it, and only as much as
  its cap. `minOutputLen(config, key)` sizes the output for the first flight with a
  CertificateRequest and for the tickets with the longest leaf.

- **Configuration.** A configuration the server accepts but cannot serve fails each handshake with `internal_error`.
  `Config.check()` reports the same up front, once (rustls refuses an inconsistent `ServerConfig` when it is built, "no kx
  groups configured"; OpenSSL `SSL_CTX_check_private_key`): no suite, no group, a group `kex` does not compute, an ALPN
  name outside 1..255 octets, `ClientAuth.schemes` without a TLS 1.3 CertificateVerify scheme, an empty authority or a
  CertificateRequest over its 2^16-1 octets of extensions, `Quic.transport_parameters` over 2^16-1, a `fixed`
  certificate `CertifiedKey.check` refuses (stale RFC 8879 copies included) and ECH keys `Ech.check` refuses. `init` stays
  infallible and does not call it; a `select` callback's keys are checked per handshake.
- **Stack.** `fromPem` wants ~110 KiB of stack (more for RSA; up to 0.8 MiB for ML-DSA, `burn.mldsa_key_burn`). A handshake
  signs and exchanges under `tls13`'s burns: up to 352 KiB for an ML-DSA-87 signature and 256 KiB for ML-KEM-1024 (ReleaseFast
  depths ×1.3; Debug frames are larger), so a small-stack worker or fiber must be sized for the keys and groups it enables.
  The `CertKeyPair` must not move after `certifiedKey()`.
- **Accepted differences, kept.** `signature_algorithms` is required (`handshake_failure` without it) even on a ClientHello
  that resumes (rustls). The second ClientHello must be the first but for RFC 8446 §4.1.2's changes: a SHA-256 over
  the first one's version, random, session id, suites, compression methods and extensions in order (all but `key_share`,
  `early_data`, `cookie`, `pre_shared_key`, `padding` and `encrypted_client_hello`, whose inner hello is the one compared) must
  match the second's, else `illegal_parameter` (Go's `illegalClientHelloChange` compares the same fields, unordered; rustls
  only the SNI and the suite's hash; tlsfuzzer `test-tls13-shuffled-extentions` wants the order kept too). ALPN may differ
  from the ticket's on a 1-RTT resumption (RFC 8446 allows it, rustls the same). `close()` before any ClientHello still lets
  a later ClientHello get a flight. `commitWrite` / `discardOutput` past their bounds are caller-contract asserts only.
  `CertifiedKey.check` runs right after certificate selection, before the
  signature scheme is matched: a misconfigured key is `internal_error` even for a client that could not have used it.
- **Client certificates.** The leaf's key and `keyUsage` are checked before the verifier (BoringSSL's order; rustls verifies
  first, so an untrusted unusable leaf gets `unsupported_certificate` here, `unknown_ca` there); a chain signature that does
  not verify is `bad_certificate` (rustls: `decrypt_error`); the chain after the leaf is kept only in `setPeerChainBuffer`'s
  buffer and only for the connection (tickets carry the leaf).
- **0-RTT.** A `ReplayGuard` shared across threads is the caller's lock. The skip budget (2^14 octets) counts ciphertext, so many
  tiny refused records can exceed it and it cannot skip a full-size early record (as rustls); empty early records cost nothing
  (a binder is needed first); a server KeyUpdate at 2^23 records could fall before the client's Finished (not reachable in
  practice).
- **Certificate compression:** a same-length replacement of the chain or a staple is not seen by `check` unless the entry carries
  its `digest` (*Wire format*).

## Anchoring

- **External:** RFC 8448 §3 — all seven protected records of the simple 1-RTT handshake
  (server EncryptedExtensions…Finished, client Finished, NewSessionTicket, both application
  data records, both close_notify alerts) sealed byte-exact and opened back, under the RFC's
  keys, IVs and sequence numbers; and the RFC's server handshake traffic secret deriving the
  key and IV it printed. Extracted from the RFC text by `tools/rfc8448_records.py`, which
  re-opens every record with Python `cryptography` (OpenSSL) before writing
  `src/record_kat_vectors.zig`.
- **External (foreign implementation):** OpenSSL 3.5.5 `s_client` over loopback TCP
  (`tools/interop.zig`, `zig build interop-tlsserver`): twelve sessions — P-256 under OpenSSL's
  defaults (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, X25519MLKEM768), TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 over X25519,
  TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 over secp256r1, P-256 under SHA-384 over X25519, P-256 over
  secp384r1, a P-384 certificate (`ecdsa_secp384r1_sha384`) over secp384r1, an Ed25519 and
  an RSA-PSS certificate, ALPN `h2` chosen from `http/1.1,h2`, no SNI, and two
  HelloRetryRequests (s_client's lone X25519 share against a server with only secp256r1 under
  SHA-384, only secp384r1 under TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256), and two KeyUpdates (the server asks
  with `update_requested` before "pong", under SHA-384 and ChaCha20; s_client answers only
  with its next application data, so the tool hands it "again") — each verified by
  s_client against the test certificate and `localhost`, with ping/pong and close_notify.
  `--capture` records every octet both ways into `src/interop_vectors.zig`;
  `src/interop_replay_test.zig` drives a server with the same seed through `Connection` over
  OpenSSL's recorded octets and requires the recorded answer byte for byte (and refuses the
  recording with one octet flipped), in every test lane.
- **External (foreign implementation):** Go 1.26.8 crypto/tls client (`tools/go_client/main.go`,
  built by the same tool with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`), twelve more sessions in the same tool and the
  same capture: Go's defaults (X25519MLKEM768, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256), TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (the server enabling only that suite: Go's TLS 1.3 suite
  order cannot be configured), secp256r1 and secp384r1 as Go's only group, a P-384, an Ed25519
  and an RSA-PSS certificate, ALPN `h2`, no SNI (verified by hand in `VerifyConnection`), and a
  server without the hybrid taking Go's X25519 share without a retry, and two HelloRetryRequests
  (Go's two default shares against a server with only secp256r1, or only secp384r1 under
  TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384; Go's `ConnectionState.HelloRetryRequest` printed). The Go client verifies the
  chain with `x509.Certificate.Verify`, prints the negotiated version, suite, group (`CurveID`)
  and ALPN — anchored on the end of the line, so `X25519` does not match `X25519MLKEM768` —
  and requires close_notify (`io.ReadAll` without an error).
- **External (foreign implementation):** whole handshakes against Zig std's
  `crypto.tls.Client` (`src/handshake_test.zig`, in one thread through in-memory pipes): an
  ECDSA P-256 certificate (self-signed test fixture, `tools/test_certs.py`) verified by the
  client against SNI `localhost`, under TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and
  TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 with X25519MLKEM768, and under X25519 and secp256r1; a request,
  a response and close_notify each way (std's client advertises `ed25519` but cannot verify it,
  so Ed25519 and RSA are covered by the OpenSSL sessions). The same handshake with P-256 and
  P-384 chains and keys loaded by `keys` from the openssl-written vectors (SEC1 and PKCS#8).
  The same pipes with the collection's `tlsclient` (std's client with `x509.verifyChain`, grown
  to Go's client options): P-256, P-384, Ed25519 and RSA-PSS certificates verified; every group
  as the lone key share × every suite (12 handshakes); tlsclient's two default shares against a
  server without the hybrid (X25519 taken, no retry) with ALPN `h2` — the client's
  `ConnectionInfo` (suite, group, ALPN, peer chain) checked against the server's
  `cipherSuite`/`negotiatedGroup`/`alpnProtocol`; and a HelloRetryRequest for secp256r1 and
  secp384r1 under each suite (6 handshakes, the client's `hello_retry_request` set).
- **External (foreign implementation):** `keys` on private keys in every PEM form the OpenSSL
  3.5.5 command line writes — `ecparam -genkey` (an `EC PARAMETERS` block, then SEC1), `ec`,
  `genpkey` (PKCS#8: P-256, P-384, Ed25519, RSA), `pkcs8 -topk8`, `rsa -traditional` (PKCS#1) —
  each with an `openssl req -x509` certificate; every key loads and matches its certificate and
  is refused (`KeyMismatch`) against every other certificate, including another P-256 one; an
  encrypted PKCS#8 key and a P-521 key are refused. `tools/key_vectors.py` →
  `src/key_vectors.zig`.
- **External (foreign implementation):** TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and
  TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which RFC 8448 does not cover — records sealed by OpenSSL
  through `cryptography` in the same tool (padding, sequence numbers up to 2^64 − 2), sealed
  byte-exact and opened back.

- **External:** RFC 8448's ClientHellos — §3 (1-RTT), §4 (resumed 0-RTT: `early_data`,
  `pre_shared_key` with one identity and binder), §5 (ClientHello1 and ClientHello2 with the
  cookie) — decode to the fields the RFC shows; §4's binder offset reproduces the RFC's "binder
  hash" (SHA-256 of the prefix). Extracted by `tools/rfc8448_messages.py`, which checks the printed
  prefix and its hash before writing `src/message_kat_vectors.zig`.

- **External:** the server's messages of RFC 8448 — §3 ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions,
  Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished; §4 ServerHello (with `pre_shared_key`) and
  EncryptedExtensions (with `early_data`); §5 HelloRetryRequest (with the cookie ClientHello2
  echoes) and the secp256r1 ServerHello; §6 CertificateRequest — rebuilt byte-exact from their
  fields by `messages` (same tool, `src/message_kat_vectors.zig`).

- **External:** RFC 8448 §6 (client authentication) end to end on the server's side: a server
  white-box at the client's second flight (the transcript through the RFC's server Finished)
  takes the RFC's client Certificate (RSA), verifies its CertificateVerify (RSA-PSS) and, under
  the RFC's client handshake traffic secret, its Finished — which covers the transcript through
  the CertificateRequest, the client's Certificate and CertificateVerify. One signature octet off
  is `decrypt_error`; the scheme not asked for, or RSA PKCS#1 v1.5, `illegal_parameter`.

- **External (foreign implementations):** client certificates from OpenSSL 3.5's `s_client`
  (`-cert`/`-key`: ECDSA P-256, RSA-2048 with RSA-PSS, Ed25519; an optional request answered
  with none; tickets after client authentication and their resumption) and Go 1.26's crypto/tls
  client (the same) against `X509Verifier` over a test client CA (`tools/client_certs.py`,
  `client_certs.zig`) — more interop sessions, captured and replayed byte-exact;
  the server must end with the presented leaf as `peerCertificate`, from the ticket on a
  resumption. In process: `tlsclient` with each key kind under every suite, no certificate
  (mandatory → `certificate_required`; optional → unauthenticated, the request's CA names and
  schemes seen by the client), refusals by the verifier (serverAuth-only EKU →
  `unsupported_certificate`, expired → `certificate_expired`, another CA → `unknown_ca`), a key
  not matching the certificate (`decrypt_error`), resumption keeping the identity, and a ticket
  without one refused under a mandatory certificate.

- **External (foreign test suite):** BoringSSL's BoGo runner (`ssl/test/runner` at 784fcafc, the last commit before it
  required Go 1.27), with `tlsserver` as its shim (`tools/bogo_shim.zig`, `zig build interop-tlsserver -- --bogo`). The
  runner's source files and the third-party files compiled into it were read in full before the first build: it spawns only
  the shim, listens on loopback only, writes only its temp test keys (under `.zig-cache`). `tools/bogo/MANIFEST` pins every
  source file's git blob hash and `--bogo` refuses a tree that differs; Go modules come from `go.sum`
  (`GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly`). `tools/bogo/passing.txt` is a ratchet: a listed test that fails or disappears fails the run.
  What is not run is disabled in `tools/bogo/config.json`, each glob with its reason (TLS 1.2 and earlier, extensions the
  server ignores, client-side, DTLS and BoringSSL-only features, deliberate divergences from BoringSSL that follow rustls).
  The shim maps the runner's flags onto `Config` (HelloRetryRequest expectations, signing preferences, server preference,
  maximum fragment, tickets and the ticket-age skew, ALPN, client-certificate verification, stapling, KeyUpdate, the
  exporter, the ECH server keys, BoringSSL's credential list, asynchronous signing, the `-resume-count` loop).
  **The rustls parity gate:** `tools/bogo/rustls_parity.py` reconstructs the tests rustls 0.23.43 passes from its
  `bogo/config.json.in` (preprocessed as the aws-lc-rs build) and its shim's option table (`bogo/src/main.rs`: a flag it
  answers 89 or does not know is not owed), with each test's flags captured by running the pinned runner once per test
  against a stub shim; the result is `tools/bogo/rustls-owed.txt`, and `--bogo` prints `GAP` for each owed test that neither
  passes nor is disabled. The list is re-derived with the script when the rustls reference moves.

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle EXTERNAL

## Fuzzing

`src/fuzz_test.zig`, harness `tlsserver-record` (`TLSSERVER_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`,
testkit's deterministic driver; `zig build --fuzz` keeps working through a `ScriptSource`). For
a random suite and traffic secret a sealed record (content length 0..1200 with the short edge
weighted, inner type, padding) opens back to the same content and type; the same record damaged
— one flipped bit, a header octet rewritten, truncation or extension, random ciphertext — or
opened under another sequence number is refused, never accepted unless the bytes are
identical, never a panic, and a refused record never advances the sequence number.
`fuzz harness: record, 300 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Harness `tlsserver-inbound`: 1–4 handshake messages (bodies up to 20,000 octets) cut into records
at random points — short cuts, whole 2^14 records and anything between — plaintext or protected
under a random suite, with compatibility CCS records at message boundaries and, when protected,
application data and a close_notify after them, fed to `Inbound.next` in random chunk sizes
(1–8 octets one time in four). The events must give back exactly the messages, the application
data and the close; the same stream damaged (a flipped bit, a rewritten header octet,
truncation, spliced random octets) never panics, and damage that reaches a protected record
carrying output is never accepted with the genuine output. `fuzz harness: inbound, 300 seeds,
reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Harness `tlsserver-hello`: a ClientHello built from a model — the fixed fields, a random subset
of nine known extensions with random well-formed bodies and up to three unknown ones, in random
order, `pre_shared_key` last one time in three — decodes to exactly the model (every list walked,
the SNI class, the binder offset); planted faults give their error (a repeated extension or
`pre_shared_key` not last: `illegal_parameter`; a 33-octet session id: `decode_error`). The same
message damaged never panics, and whatever it decodes to is walked to the end by every iterator
(bounds-checked in ReleaseSafe).

Harness `tlsserver-keys`: `keys.CertKeyPair.fromPem` on the key vectors — the key's DER with
octets rewritten (anywhere, or among the leading tags and lengths), truncated or extended and
re-armoured under its own or another key label; rebuilt from a model of its fields (version,
the scalar or seed at lengths around the curve's, own or other curve OIDs, optional `[0]` /
`[1]`, with or without the PKCS#8 wrapper, Ed25519 parameters that RFC 8410 forbids); or the
PEM text itself with octets rewritten or cut. Any outcome is a typed error, or exactly the
genuine key (compared with a genuine load); never a panic, never a leak.

Harness `tlsserver-server`: `Server` as a whole, fed the recorded OpenSSL and Go client
streams (`interop_vectors.zig`) with the recorded seed, so its output is a function of its
input. The genuine stream cut into random chunks, or fed one octet at a time, ends exactly as
recorded; truncated, it never errs and its output is a prefix of the recording; a flipped bit
in a record body never ends as recorded and, up to the client's Finished, never completes the
handshake; a flipped header bit may be refused, stall (output a prefix) or pass (output exactly
the recording — the record version octets nobody reads); random octets spliced in at a record
boundary never panic. White box: the harness takes the client's handshake traffic secret from
the server, opens the client's Finished and reseals it — damaged (a verify_data bit, one octet
short, another message type) it is refused and the handshake never completes; intact with up
to 300 octets of padding it ends as recorded. Over every run: after a failure `feed` returns
`Closed`; the alert is the last record out — plaintext and exactly `alertFor`'s fatal alert if
the server had sent nothing else, else one sealed alert record, and none after the server's own
close_notify or for an error naming none; application data never precedes `handshake_done`;
`write` before it is `NotConnected`. RSA cases run one time in ten (signing dominates).
`fuzz harness: server, 400 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Harness `tlsserver-keyupdate`: `Server` after a recorded handshake (fed through the client's
Finished), then up to 24 scripted post-handshake steps against a model client that follows
every key: client KeyUpdates of either request, whole or split over two records; client
application data, empty records included; server writes, an output left full,
`Server.keyUpdate` either way, the send key set just short of `max_records_per_key` (white
box), close_notify; and one closing refusal — an invalid request octet, a wrong length, a
KeyUpdate sharing its record with the next message, more than `max_key_updates` in a row, a
record under the client's previous key. Invariants: every server record opens under the
model's keys, in order; data arrives intact both ways; a requested KeyUpdate is out before the
server's next application data; the number of server KeyUpdates, and of those requesting one
back, is exactly what the requests, the `keyUpdate` calls and the key limit account for
(coalesced while one stays queued, dropped after close_notify); a refusal is the predicted
error, its alert the last record, sealed under the key in force; nothing is accepted after.
`fuzz harness: keyupdate, 400 seeds, reaches every outcome` runs in every test lane.

Client certificates. `tlsserver-server` and `tlsserver-keyupdate` replay the
mTLS recordings with the recorded `client_auth` (`X509Verifier` over the test client CA): the
keyupdate harness feeds the client's sealed records one at a time up to `handshake_done` (Go
sends Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished in records of their own, OpenSSL in one); the
server harness's white-box reseal takes the client's first sealed record, which now holds its
Certificate — damaged (a bit flipped anywhere in it, an octet short, a Finished where the
Certificate belongs) it is refused and the handshake never completes; repadded it ends as
recorded. Harness `tlsserver-clientauth`: a client Certificate message of zero to three real
certificates (the test client CA's leaves, the CA itself, an expired one, a P-384 server
certificate), whole — it decodes to the same chain, the leaf's key reads, the CA (keyCertSign
only) is refused for signing — or damaged (bit flips, an octet rewritten, truncation, splices),
when every certificate it still decodes to goes through `leafPublicKey` and `checkLeafKeyUsage`
(std's DER walk on an `x509.safe` copy) without a panic; then a CertificateVerify body, maybe
truncated.

Harness `tlsserver-ech`: the inner ClientHello rebuilt from a model (the outer extensions it names, `ech_outer_extensions`
replaced in one pass); every fault is refused with its error.

Harness `tlsserver-quic`: recorded Go `tls.QUICClient` sessions fed to the QUIC entry points whole, in pieces, with bits
flipped, at a wrong encryption level and cut short.

The driver prefix of every harness is `TLSSERVER_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`.

## Verification

Run: `scripts/modtest tlsserver`. External tools are not part of the test lane: `zig build interop-tlsserver` (OpenSSL 3.5
`s_client` and Go 1.26 crypto/tls sessions over loopback; `--capture` records the sessions that the tests replay),
`zig build interop-tlsserver -- --bogo` (the BoGo runner, the ratchet and the rustls parity gate, *Anchoring*),
`-- --tlsfuzzer DIR` (counts held in `tools/tlsfuzzer/baseline.tsv`: more failures than listed fail the run, other counts are a
note to update the line), `zig build bench-tlsserver` (*Performance*).

Test classes, by area:

- **Record layer** (`src/record.zig`, `src/record_kat_vectors.zig`): RFC 8448's protected records sealed byte-exact and opened
  back; the other two suites against OpenSSL-sealed records; every refusal of *Limits and refusals* (overflow, MAC, padding,
  sequence exhaustion).
- **Receive side, ClientHello, messages** (`src/inbound.zig`, `src/hello.zig`, `src/messages.zig`,
  `src/message_kat_vectors.zig`): the strictness tables of *Wire format*, RFC 8448's ClientHellos and server messages.
- **Handshake engine** (test blocks of `src/server.zig`, `src/handshake_test.zig`): whole handshakes through in-memory pipes
  against Zig std's client and `tlsclient` (every suite, group, key kind, HelloRetryRequest, tickets, client certificates,
  0-RTT, KeyUpdate, ECH, delegated credentials, offloaded signing, migration, QUIC mode), refusals and their alerts.
- **Replay** (`src/interop_replay_test.zig`, `src/interop_vectors.zig`): the recorded OpenSSL and Go sessions through
  `Connection`, byte for byte, and with one octet flipped (refused), in every test lane.
- **Keys** (`src/keys.zig`, `src/key_vectors.zig`): every PEM form the OpenSSL command line writes, matching and refusal,
  an allocation-failure sweep over every key form.
- **Mutation-derived** (`src/mutation_test.zig`, `src/mutation2_test.zig`, test blocks in the production files): each pins a
  guard that a mutant showed unguarded. Fixtures for client chains and certificates: `src/client_chain_certs.zig`,
  `src/client_certs.zig`, `src/test_certs.zig` (producers in `tools/`).
- **Dead stack** (`src/stackprobe_test.zig`, `src/interop_replay_test.zig`, ReleaseFast): the burns of `Protection`, `fromPem`,
  `Server.deserialize`, `ech.openFirst` and the handshake steps leave no secret residue; the two ML-DSA key burns (expansion,
  key-to-leaf check) are probed apart in `src/keys.zig`, each body's depth under its burn, since in `fromPem` the second
  zeroes what the first leaves.
- **Fuzz:** the harnesses of *Fuzzing*; each runs a short fixed seed set in every test lane.
- **ctgrind:** `src/ctgrind_harness.zig` through `scripts/checks/ctgrind.sh tlsserver`, rows `hs`, `app`, `ticket` and `ech`;
  counts and digests are pinned in `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module mutation run and the
  delta runs after it.

## What is deliberately not done

- **TLS 1.2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0/1.1:** never. The suites and the record format are TLS 1.3's only.
- **0-RTT without a replay guard:** `EarlyData.replay` is mandatory (BoringSSL takes early
  data with none and leaves anti-replay to the application). What early data may do is still
  the application's call (RFC 8470 for HTTP): the module only marks it (`early_data` events).
- **kTLS:** not driven by this module (measured in the web-server consumer at 41 % slower than userspace records).
  `Config.enable_secret_extraction` + `Server.extractSecrets` hand both directions' keys, IVs and sequence numbers to a
  caller that sets the socket up (rustls `enable_secret_extraction` / `dangerous_extract_secrets`); like rustls, no traffic
  secrets, so a KeyUpdate after the hand-over cannot be followed.
- **Strict parsing of extensions a TLS 1.3 server ignores** (`extended_master_secret`,
  certificate types, QUIC parameters, ECH): skipped as unknown, where rustls checks their form —
  a difference only in what malformed-but-ignored octets are refused.
- **Constant-time padding removal:** not done, as in rustls and OpenSSL (see the constant-time
  contract).
- **AES-CCM suites, brainpool and x448 / Ed448:** not offered (rustls's default provider neither); tlsfuzzer's scripts for them
  stay red by design (`tools/tlsfuzzer/baseline.tsv`). **FFDHE groups** (ffdhe2048 … ffdhe8192, `ffdhe_groups`) are served only
  when `Config.groups` enables them: they are not in `default_groups` (`src/server.zig`).
- **psk_ke (PSK without (EC)DHE) and external PSKs:** never (rustls likewise).
- **Post-handshake client authentication:** not in v1, and not in rustls either; a client's post-handshake message other than
  KeyUpdate is refused (`src/server.zig`).
- **The early exporter** (`early_exporter_master_secret`, RFC 8446 §7.5's 0-RTT variant): rustls has none on the server.
- **Compressed client certificates** (rustls `ServerConfig::cert_decompressors`: `compress_certificate` in the
  CertificateRequest and a decompressor bounded by `max_leaf_len`): BoGo has no server test for it, so parity does not ask.
  **A built-in zlib / brotli / zstd helper** for server-side compression: the caller picks (`zstd` and `brotli` are modules
  here, zlib is in std).
- **Encrypted private keys** (`ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY`, PBES2): `fromPem` refuses them (`UnsupportedKey`), as rustls
  (`PrivateKeyDer` has no encrypted form) and Go's `X509KeyPair` do; OpenSSL alone asks a password callback. A caller with
  an encrypted key decrypts it with `keycodec` (`parseEncryptedPrivateKeyPem`, then `writePrivateKeyPem`; the reader `keys.zig` and `acme` share) and
  hands the plaintext PEM over.
- **Staple parsing** (expiry, matching the leaf) and BoringSSL's server OCSP callback (`ServerOCSPCallback-*`, disabled by
  rustls too): the caller refreshes the staple; a staple per selected certificate already works through
  `Config.certificate.select`.

## Performance

Bench: `zig build bench-tlsserver` (`BENCH_ROUNDS` rounds, ReleaseFast; `tools/bench.zig`, `tools/c_bench/foreign_bench.c`,
`tools/rust_bench`). The card's `**Performance:**` line is the authoritative figure. Workloads: a full handshake with
ECDSA P-256 over X25519 and over X25519MLKEM768, a full handshake with RSA-2048 (PSS) over X25519, a resumption
(`psk_dhe_ke`, X25519) with one ticket, and sending and receiving one 16 KiB record; ratios by user-mode cycles.

All TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. The method (`tools/bench.zig`, `tools/c_bench/foreign_bench.c`):
each side records one session of its own client against its own server in memory, with the
server's randomness from a fixed seed, and a timed op is a fresh server fed the client's recorded
octets — the server's work alone (key share, signature, key schedule, records, the client's
Finished checked, the server's state set up and wiped). OpenSSL is made deterministic with a
`RAND_METHOD` (two SplitMix64 streams, client and server); both sides check before timing that
the replay sends exactly the recorded octets and negotiated the intended suite, group and
resumption. Same certificate and key, signature scheme pinned (`ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256`,
`rsa_pss_rsae_sha256`), one stateless ticket per handshake where tickets are on, no session
cache, OpenSSL's output to a null BIO and its input from a read-only memory BIO. The bulk rows
replace the connection (a timed replay) every 2048 records on both sides (~1 % of a bulk op).
The rustls side
(`tools/rust_bench`, rustls with only the aws-lc-rs provider) cannot replay — aws-lc draws its
ECDSA nonces, RSA-PSS salts and ephemeral keys from its own RNG — so each of its handshake ops is
a fresh rustls client and server in memory with only the server's calls timed (the meter stops
around the client's work); its bulk rows run on a live connection renewed every 2048 records, the
renewal's server handshake timed, as on the other sides.Not measured: ChaCha20-Poly1305 and P-384 rows, small
records (the per-record 4 KiB burn).

  buffer, `Connection.reader()`/`writer()` in place, `Server.writeSlot`/`commitWrite`, rekey bound
  `max_records_per_key`); the run itself — same traffic through the fork and through this server, outputs and
  throughput compared — has not been done.

## Open

- The KeyUpdate path holds only pointers in its own frames (HKDF and record setup burn their own) and is not in the stack probe.
- `tlsserver-server` drives `Server` only through recorded clients (plus the resealed Finished); a model client that builds
  ClientHellos from fields, as `tlsserver-hello` does, is not there.
- The cost of the per-record 4 KiB burn on small records is not measured (the bulk rows against OpenSSL libssl are 16 KiB
  records, *Performance*).
